documents.unit: Center for the Advancement of Faculty Excellence (CAFE)
documents.title: Faculty Samples (AI in the Classroom)
tiers: Generative AI use not allowed unless specifically stated as allowed
Generative AI use allowed unless specifically stated as not allowed
Generative AI use fully allowed with citation
documents.summary: A CAFE page collecting faculty-shared AI material: a Mechanical Engineering tiered AI policy (linked PDFs), a Music Industry Studies syllabus with listed permitted and forbidden AI uses, four CAFE sample syllabus statements ranging from full ban to full permission with citation, and a class discussion activity. It is sample language for instructors, not official policy.
documents.stance_why: The page offers four sample statements ('Generative AI use not allowed' through 'fully allowed with citation') and tiered examples for instructors to adopt, so it sets no single stance and leaves the choice to each instructor.

units.why: The page aims for samples to 'spark your creativity in weaving generative AI tools into your curriculum', encouraging faculty to explore AI in teaching, P63.
units.anchor: weaving generative AI tools into your curriculum
units.resolution_why: A: P56, actor admin, phase general (framing statement of the resource); B: P63, actor instructor, phase before-course, modality should. The source says the samples exist 'to spark your creativity in weaving generative AI tools into your curriculum', which urges faculty to try AI in their teaching and supports them in doing so; that is P63 (support faculty in learning AI), addressed to instructors, before-course, as a recommendation. P56 requires an institution-wide framework or principles, which a resource-page blurb is not. Final: actor=instructor, phase=before-course, modality=should, policy_type=P63, unit_stance=encourage.

units.why: The page says Dr. Hassanpour's syllabus shows 'how the different AI policy tiers are referenced and integrated' into assessments, so his course policy is organized in tiers of AI use. That is P05; the tier contents sit in linked PDFs that are not part of this saved text.
units.anchor: different AI policy tiers are referenced and integrated into course assessments and activities
units.policy: A sample ME 3250 syllabus shows how the different AI policy tiers are referenced and integrated into course assessments and activities.

units.why: The syllabus says gen AI is 'permitted' for 'checking grammar and style'. It is a permission on writing-support uses, so P18 (prose) rather than P12.
units.anchor: Checking grammar and style
units.policy: Generative AI tools (e.g. ChatGPT, Grammarly, Gemini) are permitted in this course for checking grammar and style.
units.resolution_why: Both coded P18, permit, may, during-work. A anchored the lead-in 'permitted in this course for the following activities'; B anchored the list item 'Checking grammar and style'. Same rule. Kept B's list-item anchor and A's normalized policy, which states the permission the anchor alone does not. Final: actor=student, phase=during-work, modality=may, policy_type=P18, unit_stance=permit.

units.why: The same list permits 'Brainstorming and refining your ideas', which is idea generation, matching P15.
units.anchor: Brainstorming and refining your ideas
units.policy: Generative AI tools are permitted for brainstorming and refining your ideas.

units.why: The list permits 'Finding information on your topic', using AI like a search tool to learn about a subject without producing graded answers, which matches P12.
units.anchor: Finding information on your topic
units.policy: Generative AI tools are permitted for finding information on your topic.

units.why: The list permits 'Drafting an outline to organize your thoughts', a writing-support use. I chose P18 because the outline is for a written assignment; P15 (brainstorming) fits less well because it is structuring, not idea generation.
units.anchor: Drafting an outline to organize your thoughts
units.policy: Generative AI tools are permitted for drafting an outline to organize your thoughts.
units.resolution_why: A: P18 (outline for a written assignment is writing support); B: P15 (outline is idea structuring, close to brainstorming). The source lists 'Drafting an outline to organize your thoughts' in a syllabus governing writing assignments. P15 covers idea generation and exploring approaches, whereas organizing a paper is structuring prose, so P18 follows. Brainstorming itself is coded P15 in the previous item. Final: actor=student, phase=during-work, modality=may, policy_type=P18, unit_stance=permit.

units.why: The use of AI is 'not permitted' for impersonating the student, e.g. composing discussion posts or journal entries assigned to them. It is a ban on AI producing submitted work, so P19 (P58 is about messages to staff, which this is not).
units.anchor: Impersonating you in classroom contexts
units.policy: Generative AI tools may not be used to impersonate you in classroom contexts, such as composing discussion board posts or journal entries in response to prompts assigned to you.
units.resolution_why: A: P58 (students write own course communication); B: P19 (AI may not produce submitted work). The source bans 'Impersonating you in classroom contexts, such as by using the AI tool to compose discussion board posts or journal entries in response to prompts assigned to you'. These are assignment responses submitted for the course, not messages sent to staff, so P19 fits and P58 (messages or posts to course staff) does not. Actor student, during-work, must-not, prohibit agreed. Final: actor=student, phase=during-work, modality=must-not, policy_type=P19, unit_stance=prohibit.

units.why: The syllabus says AI is 'not permitted' for 'Writing a draft of a writing assignment', which bars AI from producing the submitted work (P19).
units.anchor: Writing a draft of a writing assignment.

units.why: The syllabus bars 'Writing entire sentences, paragraphs or papers to complete class assignments', i.e. AI-produced text submitted as the student's own (P19). I coded it separately from the draft rule because it is a distinct listed prohibition.
units.anchor: Writing entire sentences, paragraphs or papers to complete class assignments

units.why: The student is told 'You are responsible for the information you submit based on an AI query', including misinformation and IP problems. This makes students answerable for submitted work (P29); P31 would stress verification, which the text does not instruct directly.
units.anchor: You are responsible for the information you submit based on an AI query
units.frag_start: You are responsible for the information
units.policy: You are responsible for the information you submit based on an AI query, for instance that it does not violate intellectual property laws or contain misinformation or unethical content.
units.resolution_why: Type, actor, phase and modality agreed. unit_stance: A neutral, B restrict. The source says 'You are responsible for the information you submit based on an AI query'; it assigns accountability without taking a position on AI use, so neutral, as for other P29 units. Final: actor=student, phase=during-work, modality=must, policy_type=P29, unit_stance=neutral.

units.why: It says 'Your use of AI tools must be properly documented and cited', a disclosure requirement attached to the work, so P24.
units.anchor: Your use of AI tools must be properly documented and cited
units.resolution_why: Actor, phase, modality and type agreed. unit_stance: A permit, B require. The passage sets a disclosure or documentation condition on AI use the syllabus otherwise allows; AI use itself is not required, so permit (codebook: require means AI use is built into or required for the work). Final: actor=student, phase=during-work, modality=must, policy_type=P24, unit_stance=permit.

units.why: It says 'Use of these tools without disclosure is academically dishonest'. Nondisclosure itself is the violation, which is P28 (not P36, since the rule is about disclosure specifically).
units.anchor: Use of these tools without disclosure is academically dishonest

units.why: It says 'Any assignment that is found to have used generative AI tools in unauthorized ways will be penalized as a violation of academic integrity'. Unauthorized AI use is classed as misconduct, P36.
units.anchor: penalized as a violation of academic integrity
units.policy: Any assignment found to have used generative AI tools in unauthorized ways is penalized as a violation of academic integrity.

units.why: The instructor says 'I will use TurnItIn, Cal Poly Pomona's plagiarism tool, on all papers routinely'. A similarity checker is used to identify misuse (P40).
units.anchor: I will use TurnItIn, Cal Poly Pomona's plagiarism tool, on all papers routinely

units.why: The instructor states 'I may use AI detection tools as well'. This is use of detection tools to identify misuse, P40. P39 (do not rely on detectors) does not fit because the text allows detectors rather than doubting them.
units.anchor: I may use AI detection tools as well

units.why: If reports show 'low originality or a high probability of AI usage', the instructor will 'ask you to meet with me and explain your work process and product'. A meeting where the student explains their work is P34; P57 (talk before escalating) is close but this text does not mention escalation.
units.anchor: I will ask you to meet with me and explain your work process and product
units.policy: If reports indicate low originality or a high probability of AI usage, the instructor will ask the student to meet and explain their work process and product.

units.why: Students must not 'simply cite the use of AI at the end of your paper' but 'cite each usage in each specific section'. This asks for marking AI use where it occurs, P27, rather than a general disclosure (P24).
units.anchor: cite each usage in each specific section as you proceed in your paper
units.frag_end: as you proceed in your paper
units.policy: Do not simply cite the use of AI at the end of your paper; cite each usage in each specific section as you proceed in your paper.
units.resolution_why: Actor, phase, modality and type agreed. unit_stance: A permit, B require. The passage sets a disclosure or documentation condition on AI use the syllabus otherwise allows; AI use itself is not required, so permit (codebook: require means AI use is built into or required for the work). Final: actor=student, phase=during-work, modality=must, policy_type=P27, unit_stance=permit.

units.why: Students who use AI must 'save your original text PRIOR to using AI' and show it on request. Keeping drafts as evidence of own work is P26 (drafts); P40 would be the instructor's checks, not the student's duty.
units.anchor: make sure to save your original text PRIOR to using AI
units.frag_end: ask you to show me your original (pre-AI) work
units.policy: If you use and cite AI in a paper, save your original text prior to using AI; the instructor will ask to see your original pre-AI work when you explain your work process and product.
units.resolution_why: Actor, phase, modality and type agreed. unit_stance: A permit, B require. The passage sets a disclosure or documentation condition on AI use the syllabus otherwise allows; AI use itself is not required, so permit (codebook: require means AI use is built into or required for the work). Final: actor=student, phase=during-work, modality=must, policy_type=P26, unit_stance=permit.

units.why: The instructor will 'ask me to show me your original (pre-AI) work' when students explain their process; this is submitting drafts on request, P26.
units.anchor: I will ask you to show me your original (pre-AI) work
units.resolution_why: Only B coded this sentence ('I will ask you to show me your original (pre-AI) work'). It is a real instructor commitment about what evidence the instructor will request when a student explains their process, so kept as P26 (keep and submit drafts or logs), as B coded it. Final: instructor, when-misuse, informs, P26, neutral.

units.why: It says 'Academic dishonesty at any stage of a project will result in at least a failing grade for that percentage of the class grade'. A penalty is named in advance, P37.
units.anchor: at least a failing grade for that percentage of the class grade
units.policy: Academic dishonesty at any stage of a project results in at least a failing grade for that percentage of the class grade, with more severe penalties possible in consultation with Student Conduct.

units.why: Sample 1 says gen AI tools 'are not permitted in this class'. The default ban on all work is P01.
units.anchor: are not permitted in this class, since such work is not entirely your own
units.policy: Generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, DALL-E, Grammarly and all other such are not permitted in this class, since such work is not entirely your own.
units.resolution_why: Actor, modality and type agreed. phase: A during-work, B general. The sentence states the default rule for AI in coursework, which students apply while doing assignments, so during-work, consistent with how the other default-stance units (P01, P02, P06) are phased. Final: actor=student, phase=during-work, modality=must-not, policy_type=P01, unit_stance=prohibit.

units.why: 'Work in this class is expected to be entirely the product of your own effort' says submitted work must be the student's own, P29.
units.anchor: expected to be entirely the product of your own effort and learning
units.resolution_why: Only B coded this sentence of the first sample ('Work in this class is expected to be entirely the product of your own effort and learning'). A folded it into the P01 ban unit. It is a distinct statement that submitted work must be the student's own, so kept as P29. unit_stance changed from require to restrict, since it does not require AI use but underpins the ban. Final: student, general, must, P29, restrict.

units.why: Sample 1 says 'The use of unauthorized AI tools will result in a failing grade for the assignment', a stated penalty (P37).

units.anchor: Some assignments in this class will specifically disallow or forbid the use of gAI tools
units.resolution_why: Actor, phase, modality and type agreed. unit_stance: A restrict, B prohibit. 'Some assignments in this class will specifically disallow or forbid the use of gAI tools': the ban covers only some assignments in an otherwise allowed setting, so restrict rather than a blanket prohibit. Final: actor=instructor, phase=course-start, modality=informs, policy_type=P04, unit_stance=restrict.

units.anchor: For these assignments, the use of unauthorized AI tools will result in a failing grade
units.resolution_why: Only B coded the penalty sentence in the third sample's second paragraph ('For these assignments, the use of unauthorized AI tools will result in a failing grade'). units.why: The third sample says some assignments forbid gAI 'because the work for those assignments must be entirely the product of your own effort and learning'. It states that submitted work must be the student's own, which is P29, the same code as the identical wording in the first sample ('expected to be entirely the product of your own effort and learning'); P41 would need an explicit claim that doing the work builds skill.

For constant comparison with the same wording in the first sample (B coded P29 there), it is P29, actor student, modality must. The clause is real and kept. units.why: Watson's class discussion concluded that AI 'like a tool (like a calculator or spellcheck) is useful, but it is cheating when students use it to replace their own thinking, voice, or effort'. This keeps students as the primary thinker (P32).
units.anchor: it is cheating when students use it to replace their own thinking, voice, or effort
units.policy: Using generative AI like a tool is useful, but it is cheating when students use it to replace their own thinking, voice, or effort.
units.resolution_why: unit_stance: A restrict, B neutral. The sentence 'it is cheating when students use it to replace their own thinking, voice, or effort' draws a line against a use of AI, so restrict. Type P32, actor student, phase general, modality informs agreed. Final: actor=student, phase=general, modality=informs, policy_type=P32, unit_stance=restrict.

units.why: Students said AI can 'be like a tutor, explaining or giving examples of concepts, checking their answers to problems, summarizing readings'. This is use as a tutor for understanding, P12.
units.anchor: AI can be like a tutor, explaining or giving examples of concepts
units.policy: Students said AI can be like a tutor, explaining or giving examples of concepts, checking their answers to problems, summarizing readings, producing samples to imitate, or helping them brainstorm ideas or outline their organization for writing tasks.
units.resolution_why: unit_stance: A permit, B neutral. 'AI can be like a tutor, explaining or giving examples of concepts' is reported as students' view of a useful use and endorses that use, so permit. Type P12 agreed. Final: actor=student, phase=general, modality=informs, policy_type=P12, unit_stance=permit.

units.why: Watson asked students to discuss 'When is (generative) AI useful in education?' and 'When is using (generative) AI cheating in education?' so the class articulates appropriate use together. This is the instructor communicating and building expectations at course start, informs. No type covers co-creating the rules with students (P35 is about redesigning assignments and grading), so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: Collaborating with students to articulate appropriate use of gAI
units.policy: Jennie Watson has the class discuss when generative AI is useful and when using it is cheating, to articulate appropriate use of gAI.
units.uncovered_note: Instructor co-creates the class's AI expectations with students through a discussion of when AI is useful and when it is cheating.
units.resolution_why: A: P35; B: UNCOVERED. The passage is a class discussion in which students and instructor work out when generative AI is useful and when it is cheating. P35 covers redesigning assignments or grading around AI; this activity is about building the AI expectations with students, which no type covers. Final: UNCOVERED, with a note. Final: actor=instructor, phase=course-start, modality=informs, policy_type=UNCOVERED, unit_stance=neutral.

documents.unit: Center for the Advancement of Faculty Excellence (CAFE)
documents.title: About Navigating AI in the Classroom at CPP
documents.summary: A short CAFE framing page for faculty. It says no official university AI policy exists, lists concerns (integrity, over-reliance, accuracy and bias) and benefits, and describes CAFE workshops and consultations.
documents.stance_why: The page says 'no official university policy regarding gAI exists yet' and 'does not represent any official policy', and only lists concerns, benefits and support for faculty, so it sets no stance and leaves decisions to instructors.

units.why: The guide says 'no official university policy regarding gAI exists yet' and that it 'does not represent any official policy'. No type covers a statement that the institution has no policy, so I used UNCOVERED; it also marks the guide as non-binding.
units.anchor: no official university policy regarding gAI exists yet
units.frag_end: address common faculty concerns and explore its potential benefits
units.uncovered_note: Statement that no official university-wide AI policy exists and that the guidance does not represent official policy by governing bodies such as the Academic Senate.
units.resolution_why: Both coded UNCOVERED, general, informs, neutral. Kept, with uncovered_note: no type covers an institution stating it has no official AI policy. Final: actor=admin, phase=general, modality=informs, policy_type=UNCOVERED, unit_stance=neutral.

units.why: It lists a teaching concern: 'Unapproved use of gAI to complete assignments can compromise learning and constitute plagiarism'. Unapproved use is classed as plagiarism, P36.
units.anchor: Unapproved use of gAI to complete assignments can compromise learning and constitute plagiarism

units.why: It warns 'Students may become overly reliant on gAI, hindering their development of critical thinking and research skills'. Reliance undermines skill-building, P41.
units.anchor: Students may become overly reliant on gAI, hindering their development of critical thinking
units.resolution_why: Type P41, phase, modality agreed. unit_stance: A restrict, B neutral. 'Students may become overly reliant on gAI, hindering their development of critical thinking' is a concern that argues against over-use, so restrict. Final: actor=all, phase=general, modality=informs, policy_type=P41, unit_stance=restrict.

units.why: It says 'gAI outputs can be inaccurate or biased, requiring careful evaluation and fact-checking'. This is the verify-output warning, P31.
units.anchor: gAI outputs can be inaccurate or biased, requiring careful evaluation and fact-checking

units.why: It says 'gAI can help students brainstorm ideas, overcome writer's block, and access diverse sources for research'. A positive use for brainstorming, P15.
units.anchor: gAI can help students brainstorm ideas, overcome writer's block, and access diverse sources

units.why: It says 'gAI can provide personalized support to students, tailoring content and practice to their needs'. Personalized support is tutor-like; P12 chosen over P14 because the passage is about support, not generating practice sets.
units.anchor: gAI can provide personalized support to students, tailoring content and practice
units.resolution_why: A: P12 (tutor-like support); B: P14 (practice and study aids). The source says 'gAI can provide personalized support to students, tailoring content and practice to their needs'. The passage is about support tailored to the student, which is tutoring; P14 is for generating practice problems, study guides or reviews, which the passage does not describe. Final P12. Final: actor=student, phase=during-work, modality=informs, policy_type=P12, unit_stance=encourage.

units.why: It says 'gAI can automate repetitive tasks, freeing up faculty time'. This is a use of AI by instructors in their teaching work, P59.
units.anchor: gAI can automate repetitive tasks, freeing up faculty time

units.policy: CAFE offers workshops on gAI for teaching and learning, covering effective gAI tools and strategies for classroom integration.
